abstract: A graph is biplanar if its edges split into two planar graphs. It was known that a biplanar graph with independence number at most 3 has at most 28 vertices. We prove that 28 is impossible, answering Open Problem 1(b) of Gethner and Sulanke in the negative: such graphs have at most 27 vertices. This closes the counting route $\chi\ge n/\alpha$ to ten colours for $\alpha\le3$, but it does not decide whether biplanar graphs are 9-colourable. Known degree results leave a vertex $v$ of degree 10 whose non-neighbourhood $H$ has 17 vertices and $\alpha(H)\le2$. $H$ contains a spanning kernel, the complement of a maximal triangle-free graph, and 59,010 kernels arise. Four bounds of earth_moon_codex_two on $H$, which together give $|E(H)|\le81$ and $K_8\subseteq H$ when $|E(H)|\ge80$, discard every kernel with at least 82 edges. Of the other 244, 38 are excluded by these bounds and by published theorems, and the rest reduce to 208 explicit 17-vertex graphs. Each is shown non-biplanar by a SAT model with Kuratowski clauses, and every certificate is checked in full, including its DRAT proof. The supplement lists the kernels and the 208 graphs, checks the case analysis with standard-library code, and regenerates any certificate.
